Food now comes from a shop, and a household's food does not pass through other households.
parameters.gap_statement: A forager ate food that others in the camp had caught, carried or cooked, and others ate theirs, among people who knew who gave what. Among 37,193 older Japanese adults followed for three years, men living alone who usually ate alone had 2.36 times the rate of new depressive symptoms of men living alone who ate with others, after adjustment for income, health, nutrition and other factors (ext 3684); in a cross-sectional study, people who lived with their families yet ate alone had the highest odds of depressive symptoms (ext 3583).

Strongest study: Kitanishi 1998 (ext 1586), 103 days of counts in two Aka camps; main weakness: one ethnographer in one region, and the 20% and 75% figures rest on his estimate of what stayed in the pot. Modern side: the US time-use series (De Neve et al. 2025, ext 1603); main weakness: one country, in a report chapter without journal review. The links between shared meals and life ratings (ext 1602, 1604) are cross-sectional and both sources leave the direction open. parameters.name: Who picks the partner (kin-arranged marriage)
parameters.eea_baseline: In most forager societies parents or close kin arranged marriages. In Apostolou's coding of 190 forager societies, arrangement by parents or close kin was the main way to marry in 85%, and marriage involved an exchange between the two families (brideservice, brideprice) in 80%. A phylogenetic reconstruction puts arranged marriage at least as far back as the migrations out of Africa. Courtship also existed: 3 of the 8 African forager societies in the sample marry by courtship, so the oldest African pattern is open. How much say the young people had is not coded in any source read; Hadza men and women state clear preferences for a spouse. Among the Tsimane forager-horticulturalists of Bolivia, asked why they married their spouse, women most often answered that they married against their will (37.6%, ext 5850). Among the Ju/'hoansi, more than 60% of brides said they had been mildly or strongly reluctant about their first marriage, wives started 90% of the divorces in first marriages, and after a divorce women had much more say in choosing the next husband (Wiessner 2009 as reported by Scelza 2013, ext 5855). Among Himba pastoralists of Namibia, 9% of women's first marriages were love matches against 62% of second marriages (ext 5856). Across five non-Western societies, scores for intimacy, passion and commitment did not differ between arranged and free-choice marriages in the pooled data (ext 5859).

parameters.name: The pool of possible partners
parameters.eea_baseline: A forager chose from a small pool of people who were known before anything started. Among the Aka, the area a person explores over a lifetime, looking for a mate, visiting kin and hunting, reaches about 50 km (half the places an Aka adult has visited lie within 30 km of camp, ext 3204) and holds about 700 people they can meet and get to know. The lifetime pool of individually known people was about 1,000 in the Ache and Hadza. Possible partners came with a known family and a reputation.
parameters.modern_default: Online, the pool is effectively unbounded and made of strangers. On one large US dating site, attention was very unequal: most users got a handful of first messages at most while a few got hundreds (one woman in New York got 1,504 in a month). Men and women mostly wrote to people about 25% more desirable than themselves, and men writing to more desirable women got replies at most 21% of the time.
parameters.gap_statement: The pool grew from hundreds of known people to an open-ended list of strangers judged from a profile. Attention concentrates on a few, and most people's approaches go unanswered.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested once. Ancestral value: one Aka ethnography (Hewlett 2005, ext 841) and one model-based estimate in two populations (Hill et al. 2014). Modern side: one site, four US cities, one month (Bruch and Newman 2018). No peer-reviewed data on how unequal likes or matches are on swipe apps was found. Evidence cited (abstract or book only): ext 841. Added 19 Nov 2026. That a partner was known to the group beforehand is inferred from the size of the pool; no study records it, so that step is argued, not yet tested. Distance between spouses grows as population thins, among foragers and among farmers (MacDonald and Hewlett 1999, ext 1744, abstract only). Among the Tsimane the preferred spouse is known kin (ext 1732).

evidence.author_quote: Among the Ache and Hadza, frequent visiting and long lifespans mean that adults typically interact with more than three hundred same-sex adults during their lifetimes. evidence.content: Among Ache and Hadza foragers, lifetime same-sex interaction exceeds 300 adults, implying a lifetime "social universe" of about a thousand individuals once opposite-sex adults and children are included.

evidence.author_quote: Additionally, close companions often interact with a somewhat different set of individuals, so that the total number of indirect interactants that each individual hears about repeatedly in detailed stories, and could expect to possibly meet some time during their lifetime is clearly more than 1,000. evidence.content: The lifetime pool of individually-known interactants is clearly >1,000 - which Hill et al. explicitly note is far above the ~150 figure (the Dunbar number) that was extrapolated from primate brain / social-group-size regressions.

parameters.name: Marriage system (mostly one spouse at a time, often several over a life, polygyny allowed in most societies)
parameters.eea_baseline: Most societies in the ethnographic record permitted a man more than one wife (about 85%), but in forager societies most marriages were monogamous. In 87% of 190 forager societies fewer than 20% of men were married polygynously; among tropical African foragers polygyny runs from 3% to 20%; among Savanna Pume foragers 11% of men and 20% of women are ever married polygynously. Men contributing more food went with more monogamy. Serial pairing was common: among the !Kung and Ache, men and women had children with more than one partner. Over a life, many people had several spouses: Ache women in the pre-contact forest period averaged 12.1 husbands and about 63% of Ache children had a secondary father (ext 1730); perhaps 20% of Hadza stay married to the same person for life (ext 1729). Among the Tsimane of Bolivia, forager-horticulturalists, fewer than 20% of marriages ended in divorce (15 of 76 marriages begun more than 20 years before), most often in the first year, and 5 to 10% of men were married polygynously, almost always to two sisters (ext 5849). Of 25 forager populations in a meta-analysis of reproductive skew, 10 had normative monogamy, 13 tolerated but rare polygyny and 2 normative polygyny (ext 3066). Across 142 societies of the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample, the rule on how many wives a man may have tracked the share of men and of women actually married polygynously (r .76 and .81, ext 5835). Starkweather and Hames identified 53 societies outside the classical Himalayan and Marquesan area that permit polyandry, one woman with more than one husband, and report that it is most common in egalitarian societies (ext 5833). Genetic studies estimate more breeding women than breeding men: a female to male ratio of 2.1 (San) to 12.5 (Basque) in one study of six populations (ext 5841), and 1.33 (East Asians) to 2.63 (Yoruba) in corrected HapMap estimates (ext 5842, 5843). Hammer and colleagues read the excess as polygyny, formal and effective; Labuda and colleagues read their corrected values as within the range of monogamous or serially monogamous societies, while also overlapping with polygynous ones.
parameters.modern_default: Law imposes one spouse at a time in most states (Japan from 1880, China 1953, India 1955, Nepal 1963). Serial pairing through divorce and new partners continues.
parameters.gap_statement: Small gap. Forager practice was already mostly one spouse at a time with some polygyny and remarriage; modern law removes the polygynous minority. Forager marriages often ended: across ten forager and forager-farmer populations reported divorce rates run from 18% (Agta) to nearly every couple (north Alaskan Inuit), and the reviewers put the general level at a quarter to a third of marriages or more, with remarriage common (ext 1728). The rates were counted differently in each population, so they cannot be averaged or set against a modern rate. Where polygyny is practised today: in 56 villages of northern Tanzania, within villages polygyny was not significantly related to food security, height-for-age or weight-for-height (ext 5845); among the Dogon of Mali the hazard of death by age 5 was higher in work-eat groups with more married women per married man in villages 1 to 8, and only in village 9, exceptionally large and wealthy, did polygyny show no adverse effect (ext 5848).
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested many times for 'mostly monogamous with some polygyny in foragers' (Apostolou coding via Walker et al. 2011; Pume demography, Schacht and Kramer 2019; African forager ethnographies via Henrich et al. 2012; Marlowe 2003, ext 767). Any single number is one study. Keep 'permitted' (85% of societies) apart from 'practised' (a minority of forager marriages). Evidence cited (abstract or book only): ext 767, 768. Divorce and number of mates, added 19 Nov 2026: Hewlett et al. 2023 (ext 1728, 1729) and Winking and Gurven 2011 (ext 1730) compile the original demographic studies; main weakness: each team counted divorce differently. Added 26 Nov 2026 (answers job 3): Gurven et al. 2009 for the Tsimane (ext 5849); Ross et al. 2023 for the 25 forager populations (ext 3066); White and Burton 1988 for rule against practice (ext 5835); Starkweather and Hames 2012 for polyandry, abstract only (ext 5833); Hammer et al. 2008, Labuda et al. 2010 with its erratum, and Lohmueller et al. 2010 for the genetic ratio, which agree that breeding women outnumbered breeding men and disagree on by how much (ext 5841, 5842, 5843); Dupanloup et al. 2003 propose from Y-chromosome diversity that humans were essentially polygynous during much of their history, an interpretation of genetic data, abstract only (ext 5844); Lawson et al. 2015 and Strassmann 2011 for children in polygynous households (ext 5845, 5848). Each is one study or one group.

parameters.name: Number of children and spacing
parameters.eea_baseline: Forager women who lived through their reproductive years had about six births: Ache 8.2, Agta 6.9, Hadza 6.2, Hiwi 5.5, Ju/'hoansi 4.3; the mean across 75 natural-fertility societies was 5.98. Births were spaced about 3 to 4 years apart (hunter-gatherer average 3.7 years). About a third of forager women survived to complete their fertility. With pregnancy and long breastfeeding, menstrual cycles were few: among the Dogon, natural-fertility farmers, a woman had about 100 menstruations in her life.

parameters.modern_default: World births per woman fell from 4.84 in 1950 to 2.23 in 2021, and fell in every country. Among European women born in 1960, 10% (Greece, Spain) to 20% (Germany) had no child, a level also seen in women born around 1900. A US woman with three births has about three times the Dogon count of menstruations.
parameters.gap_statement: Fewer children, fewer pregnancies and far more menstrual cycles. Each birth lowered the relative risk of breast cancer by 7.0 percent and each 12 months of breastfeeding by a further 4.3 percent across 47 studies in 30 countries, and the authors estimate that the births and breastfeeding usual in developing countries until recently would cut the cumulative risk by age 70 in developed countries from 6.3 to 2.7 per 100 women (Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer 2002). Women in the top quarter of lifetime ovulatory cycles had 1.81 times the odds of ovarian cancer of women in the bottom quarter (Pelucchi et al. 2007). parameters.name: Alloparental care supply (a village, not a dyad)
parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral human infants were not raised by a mother alone but by a network of allomothers - fathers, grandmothers, older siblings, and trusted non-kin - who shared both direct care (holding, carrying, soothing) and provisioning (food). Hrdy argues that humans are a cooperatively breeding ape (ext 22): unlike other African apes, whose mothers nurture infants essentially on their own, hominin mothers relied on groupmates to protect, care for, and provision their unusually slow-maturing, costly young. A human child requires on the order of 13 million calories from birth to independence, and humans breed faster (every 3-4 years) than chimpanzees and orangutans (about every 5.5 and 7.7 years; gorillas breed about every 3.8 years, Galdikas and Wood 1990, ext 3519) while producing larger, slower-maturing babies - a life-history paradox Hrdy argues is solvable only by shared provisioning (ext 401). Across foraging ethnography, infants were handled by people other than the mother from shortly after birth: among the Hadza, the mother does roughly 69% of the time children aged four and under were held (ext 2128) and allomothers the rest; !Kung infants have the mother's entire social world available with intense face-to-face interactions from girls; among the Trobriand Islanders, who are horticulturalists, infants are suckled by lactating allomothers. The infant's evolved expectation is a reliable surround of multiple invested caregivers, not a single isolated dyad.

eea_value.note: Specific aggregate 'alloparent count ~4+' and a generic '40-50% of care delivered by allomothers' figure are NOT verbatim-grounded in Cor's extractions; the Hadza ~69/31 mother/allomother holding split, the 57/43 split of an infant's direct care between mothers and other people in one study of Savanna Pume hunter-gatherers and one Yucatec Maya farming village (ext 811), and the qualitative multi-caregiver pattern are. Numbers given are the extraction-supported anchors, not an asserted universal mean.

parameters.name: Caregiver continuity and reliability (present, not merely countable)
parameters.eea_baseline: Attachment is not a single dyadic bond but secure attachment to one or more trusted caretakers, Bowlby's design refined by Hrdy to plural figures, and human infants are equipped with traits (cuteness, prolonged eye contact, social smiling) for recruiting the attention of potential caretakers. Crucially, maternal commitment itself is contingent: for a cooperatively breeding mammal, the capacity to conceive is only part of the equation; the mother must be able to carry through to rearing independence, which she assesses against perceived alloparental support. Touch is part of this continuity. In the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample the mother slept in the same room as her infant in every one of the 173 societies coded, and in the same bed in at least 76 (ext 705). Field argues that the skin is the first and the largest sense organ to develop prenatally (ext 296). The expectation is not a list of relatives but caregivers who are reliably, physically present across time.
parameters.modern_default: In the United States of the late 1970s infants spent little time in body contact with caregivers, their movements were restricted by playpens, high chairs or cribs, and separate sleeping was regularly recommended (ext 3145); all Euro-American infants observed in Washington, D.C. had their own crib in their own room (ext 3151), and of the 18 US infants, 15 slept near their mothers until 3 to 6 months of age, when most were moved to a separate room (ext 3435). Caregivers may be nominally present (counted on paper) yet not reliably, responsively available in the moment-to-moment way the regulatory system expects.
parameters.gap_statement: The mismatch is between caregiver reliability/continuity as an experienced, present regulatory input and a modern environment that often supplies caregivers who are countable but not dependably present. Because maternal investment and infant attachment are both calibrated to perceived caregiver reliability (M9, R1), low continuity is not neutral: it degrades the secure-base scaffolding and the touch-mediated regulation the infant evolved to expect, even when the number of caregivers on paper looks adequate.
parameters.resolution_unit: Reliable, present caregiver supply - responsive caregivers actually and repeatedly available across time, including continuity of body contact - NOT a count of designated or genealogically-related caregivers. The naive reading (enough named caregivers exist) misleads; what regulates the infant is dependable presence.
parameters.confidence_note: The extractions for the continuity/reliability claim (276, 281, 402) are graded theoretical (Hrdy/Bowlby interpretive synthesis); the forager care findings 701, 702 and 842 are graded thin; the touch items are 296 (theoretical), 294 (cross_species, Harlow/Suomi) and 705 (replicated). The row is graded argued, not yet tested. The specific operationalization of 'continuity' as a measured construct is not pinned to a number, hence eea_value is null and the parameter is qualitative.

parameters.name: Mixed-age child playgroups as developmental input
parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral children developed social competence through play with a mixed-age band of other children - younger and older mixed together - rather than under continuous adult supervision or in age-segregated peer cohorts. Rough-and-tumble play during the juvenile period is a dedicated developmental input: in the mammalian design, play is a distinct emotional system (Panksepp's PLAY) and, in rats, play experience physically tunes the maturing prefrontal cortex (ext 212), refining, as Pellis and Pellis propose (ext 216), the circuits that later dampen the amygdala and support emotional regulation. Critically, the AMOUNT and quality of play partners matters: female rats raised with more play partners show progressively greater play experience and corresponding PFC development, and even the untreated playmates of more-playful partners tended to have greater cortical thickness (ext 220) - play is a partnered input, so a richer multi-partner (and, in the human case, multi-age) play environment is the expected calibrating stimulus.
parameters.modern_default: Modern childhood compresses or eliminates free mixed-age play: age-segregated grade cohorts and daycare, adult-structured and supervised activities, indoor screen-based leisure, reduced unsupervised outdoor roaming, and safety norms that discourage rough-and-tumble.
parameters.gap_statement: The mismatch is between mixed-age, self-organized, physically-active play as the evolved calibrating input for the juvenile prefrontal cortex (M4, embedded in the alloparental child-minding network, M9) and a modern environment that supplies age-segregated, adult-structured substitutes. In rats, play with partners shapes the developing cortex (Pellis & Pellis 2009, ext 212, 220). Cor reads reduced free play in children as a missing developmental input. In children, general risky outdoor play (13 studies) and places that allow risky play (21 studies) went with better physical, mental, social and cognitive outcomes in a review of 74 studies (Ramsden et al. 2026, ext 5097), and children whose parents reported more time playing adventurously before the pandemic had slightly fewer internalising symptoms and more positive affect during the first Covid-19 lockdown (Dodd, Nesbit and FitzGibbon 2023, ext 5104).
parameters.resolution_unit: Self-directed, mixed-age, physically-active free play actually engaged in - partnered play experience - NOT adult-structured activities, solitary screen play, or scheduled lessons that occupy time without delivering the rough-and-tumble, role-reversal, peer-negotiated input the circuits expect.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Mixed-age child playgroups are documented across forager societies in two systematic reviews (Lew-Levy et al. 2017, 2018). The label covers the ancestral value only: the claim that age mixing shapes development rests on rat work and is untested in humans. In monkeys, isolates raised alone for 6 months recovered with younger partners (ext 1887). A review of tests of pretend play found weak and inconsistent evidence that it causes the developmental gains credited to it (Lillard et al. 2013, ext 762); the tests it reviews are mostly adult-led play training in preschools, which is not the self-organised play this row describes.

parameters.name: Multigenerational presence (older people inside the band's giving and getting)
parameters.eea_baseline: Older people kept a place in the band's giving and getting. They gave food (ext 2063, 3088), care (ext 2084) and knowledge (ext 3827) where they could, and they were given to (ext 3088, 3665). The project's position: reciprocity runs across the whole life, so a grandmother who gave for a lifetime holds her place when she takes. What older people gave differed by group. Among the Hadza, grandmothers foraged most when their newest grandchild was youngest (ext 2063). Among the Tsimane, net food flowed down the generations: grandmothers gave a net 117 kcal a day to their grandchildren and grandfathers 223, into their 70s (ext 3088). Among the Aka, care by others, largely grandmothers, lowered mothers' work by up to 216 kcal over nine hours (ext 2084). Tsimane adults named grandparents most often as the source of the stories they knew (ext 3827). Among the Ache and Hiwi, older women did not contribute food that eased the deficits of middle-aged couples raising children, and about 10 percent of middle-aged Ache women lived with their own mothers (ext 2301). Agta adults named old age among the needs that decided whom they gave to in an experimental sharing game (ext 3665). The grandmother hypothesis (and Lieberman's active-grandparent corollary) holds that the long human life after the last birth (among 52 wild mammal species, longer than chance only in humans, orcas and short-finned pilot whales, ext 3722) was selected for and made possible by older adults remaining physically active to help rear children, grandchildren, and other young kin, increasing inclusive fitness through kin-selected provisioning. Older people are thus part of the alloparental supply: a band of several generations in which the old kept a place in the exchange and were no absent generation.
parameters.modern_default: Among US adults aged 25 or over with a living parent or adult child, 13.2% lived with a parent or adult child, 74.8% had the nearest one within 30 miles and 6.8% had the nearest one 500 miles or more away (ext 4204). In ten European countries 58 percent of grandmothers and 49 percent of grandfathers looked after a grandchild in the past year (Hank and Buber 2009, ext 4209).
parameters.gap_statement: The mismatch is between older people who keep a place in the daily giving and getting of a band of several generations (M9, M3) and the modern default of grandparents who live apart from it.
parameters.resolution_unit: Older relatives present and inside the family's daily giving and getting: giving care, food or knowledge where they can, and being provided for. NOT mere grandparental existence or living-relative count. A surviving grandmother several time zones away does not fill the place a band of several generations gave her.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (22 Nov 2026): tested many times for what the row claims, that older people were present and inside the giving and getting. Post-reproductive survival is common across foragers (Gurven and Kaplan 2007, ext 723), and food and care from older people were measured by separate teams among the Hadza (ext 2063), the Tsimane (ext 3088) and the Aka (ext 2084); main weakness: each flow is measured in one population, and among the Ache and Hiwi older women did not ease the deficits of middle-aged couples (ext 2301). The grandmother hypothesis in the baseline is an evolutionary reading, which the label does not cover; on child survival, across 17 studies in patrilineal populations surviving maternal grandparents went with lower child mortality and paternal grandparents did not (Strassmann and Garrard 2011, ext 3536). On child growth, among 127 Aka children grandmothers were the allomother most linked to better nutritional status, clearest from 9 months to 3 years (Meehan, Helfrecht and Quinlan 2014). On food the row states a project position (21 Nov 2026): a grandmother who gave for a lifetime need not feed anyone to hold her place. Measured flows differ by group: down the generations among the Tsimane (ext 3088); Hadza grandmothers foraged more when grandchildren were youngest (ext 2063); among the Ache and Hiwi older women did not ease the deficits of middle-aged couples (ext 2301).

evidence.author_quote: In order to elucidate the links between exercise and aging, I propose a corollary to the grandmother hypothesis, which I call the active grandparent hypothesis. According to this idea, human longevity was not only selected for but also made possible by having to work moderately during old age to help as many children, grandchildren, and other younger relatives as possible to survive and thrive. That is, while there might have been selection for genes (as yet unidentified) that help humans live past the age of fifty, there was also selection for genes that repair and maintain our bodies when we are physically active. As a result, many of the mechanisms that slow aging and extend life are turned on by physical activity, especially as we get older. Human health and longevity are thus extended both by and for physical activity.

parameters.name: Affective (C-tactile) contact frequency and skin-to-skin time
parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral infants lived in near-continuous bodily contact: carried on the body, fed at short intervals, and held skin-to-skin for much of the day (ext 2082), with frequent touch from the mother and a wider circle of caregivers. Field argues that the skin is the first and largest sense organ and that the fetus is already continuously stimulated in utero (ext 296). Skin-to-skin/carried contact was the species-typical default, not an intervention.

eea_value.note: No defensible single ancestral 'touches-per-hour' number; cross-cultural touch frequency ranges enormously (0-180+ contacts between two people sharing coffee in cafés in four cities per Jourard, ext 295), so the EEA value is a high-contact regime with a floor, not a point estimate
eea_value.infant_contact: near-continuous (carried, co-sleeping, fed at frequent short intervals)

parameters.modern_default: In the United States of the late 1970s infants spent little time in body contact with caregivers and their movements were restricted by playpens, high chairs or cribs (ext 3145), and Euro-American infants were held less than Aka and Ngandu infants and were more often alone (ext 3151); personal-space norms and screen-mediated interaction strip casual affective touch from daily adult life.
parameters.gap_statement: Touch deprivation produces growth hormone suppression in rat pups and immune breakdown in infant monkeys (ext 3508, 294); even in non-extreme modern life the loss of moderate-pressure affective touch removes a direct oxytocin/vagal/cortisol-regulating input. Critically, affective touch is the one ancestral channel that remote, volumetric, or screen-based technology cannot deliver: it requires physical skin contact.
parameters.resolution_unit: Reliable supply of moderate-pressure, skin-to-skin/affective (C-tactile) contact, especially in infancy and under stress; NOT incidental or light/ticklish touch (light touch does not produce the physiological response) and NOT a raw count of any contact.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Near-continuous infant carrying and frequent nursing are documented in !Kung, Aka and Efe, with breastfeeding into the second or third year across non-industrial societies (Sellen 2007). The adult high-touch part rests on modern observation and is argued. The kangaroo-care mortality benefit applies to stabilized low-birthweight infants (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.39-0.92; Conde-Agudelo & Diaz-Rossello 2016, ext 618) and is largest in low- and middle-income settings.

evidence.author_quote: The skin is the first and the largest sense organ to develop prenatally. The fetus is suspended in amniotic fluid and receives active stimulation from the fluid and the mother and others as they touch her abdomen. The fetus becomes increasingly active as this happens. The fetus also touches itself by thumb sucking and grasping the umbilical cord. The fetus gets a continuous massage for the entire nine months from both the amniotic fluid and the mother's insides. In addition, a pregnant woman naturally massages her baby in the womb. Touch alters oxytocin (an estrogen-dependent chemical), which relaxes the individual, promotes touch, encourages bonding, triggers milk letdown during breastfeeding, and sets off the uterine contractions that accompany childbirth.

parameters.name: Co-sleeping
parameters.eea_baseline: In every one of the 173 societies coded in the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample, the mother slept in the same room as her infant, and in at least 76 of them in the same bed (ext 705); the sample spans foragers, farmers, herders and others, not foragers alone. parameters.gap_statement: Solitary infant sleep removes the nighttime proximity of the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample, where the mother slept in the same room as her infant in every one of the 173 societies coded, and in the same bed in at least 76 (ext 705). parameters.name: Dawn/dusk light gradient with genuine nocturnal darkness as circadian entrainment signal
parameters.eea_baseline: Across evolutionary history the human circadian pacemaker (suprachiasmatic nucleus) was entrained by a high-amplitude natural light-dark cycle: bright daytime illumination, a dusk dimming, and then real darkness for the duration of the biological night, with only firelight (low) as evening illumination. In wrist-sensor recordings of Hadza, San and Tsimane adults, no group went to sleep near sunset: sleep began on average 3.3 hours after sunset (ext 2224). The operative signal is the timing and spectral content of light at the day-night transition.

parameters.gap_statement: The modern light environment inverts the ancestral pattern on both ends: too little bright light by day, too much blue-enriched light at night. This delays circadian phase, compresses the biological night, and decouples internal time from external solar time.
parameters.resolution_unit: Spectral timing of light exposure at the day-night transition (dusk dimming + nocturnal darkness).

parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestrally, sleep occurred within a phase relationship to the solar/circadian night: onset about three hours after sunset (3.3 hours on average among Hadza, San and Tsimane, ext 2224; about three hours in rural Haiti without electricity, ext 3903), offset near or before dawn, with the sleep episode anchored to internal circadian time. parameters.modern_default: Industrial schedules set wake times by clock and alarm rather than by internal time, producing chronic 'social jetlag' - a standing offset between the endogenous circadian phase and the socially imposed sleep window. parameters.gap_statement: The mismatch is primarily one of phase, not amount. Independently of sleep duration, misalignment between biological and social clocks is associated with metabolic harm (e.g. social jetlag raises overweight odds and predicts BMI in the overweight, with an effect more than half that of sleep duration, after controlling for duration itself). Across 43 studies of 231,648 people, social jetlag went with higher body mass index and 1.2 times the odds of overweight (Arab et al. 2024), and in the high-quality studies of a review of 68 with higher body mass index, waist, systolic blood pressure and HbA1c (Bouman et al. 2023). In 60,977 UK adults, regular sleep and wake times predicted lower mortality more strongly than sleep duration did (Windred et al. 2024). Chasing a duration number while ignoring phase misses the operative variable.
parameters.resolution_unit: Sleep timing/phase - the alignment of the sleep episode to internal circadian night - NOT sleep duration.

parameters.name: Falling evening ambient temperature as a second sleep-onset cue
parameters.eea_baseline: In Hadza, San and Tsimane, the sleep period consistently occurred during the nighttime period of falling environmental temperature and ended near the nadir of daily ambient temperature (ext 745). This descending thermal ramp coincides with the endogenous evening fall in core body temperature that accompanies sleep onset, plausibly acting as a second zeitgeber-like onset cue alongside light.
parameters.modern_default: Climate-controlled indoor environments hold ambient temperature roughly constant across the 24-hour cycle, removing the nighttime period of falling environmental temperature (ext 745).
parameters.gap_statement: By flattening the daily thermal cycle, modern housing removes a candidate onset cue, potentially leaving light as the sole (and now corrupted) entrainment channel. In Hadza, San and Tsimane the sleep period consistently occurred during the nighttime period of falling environmental temperature (ext 745).
parameters.resolution_unit: Direction and timing of the nighttime ambient-temperature change (falling during the sleep period, ext 745), not absolute thermostat setpoint or daytime comfort.

parameters.name: Daily incidental movement load
parameters.eea_baseline: Across a foraging day, adults covered substantial ground on foot as a structural side-effect of acquiring food: Hadza men walk about 11.4 km a day and women about 5.8 km (Pontzer et al. 2012, GPS; ext 2430), and the women also dig for several hours (Lieberman 2021, ext 196). Activity was modest in intensity and embedded: light chores, sit-to-stand transitions (~50 a day, similar to ~38 for European adults; ext 289), and active resting postures (squatting, kneeling) that sustain low-level lower-limb muscle activity. Hunter-gatherer PAL is only modestly above a Western desk worker's (~1.8-1.9 vs ~1.6), so the EEA baseline is not 'extreme exertion'. It is 'movement is the unavoidable medium of subsistence.'

parameters.modern_default: Movement has been extracted from subsistence and re-inserted, if at all, as discretionary 'exercise': set-aside, planned, dose-prescribed (e.g. 150 min/week guidelines), and separated from the rest of a chair-bound, motor-transported, indoor day. Hadza women took about twice and Hadza men about three times the daily steps of smartphone users aged 18 to 75 in a 111-nation sample from middle- and high-income countries (ext 3418).
parameters.gap_statement: The gap is not a calorie or PAL gap (these are surprisingly close). Hadza adults spent 134.92 minutes a day in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (ext 2233). Average sedentary bout duration is similar in Hadza and industrialized adults (~15 min), and Hadza spend about 18% of nonambulatory time squatting and 12.5% kneeling; squatting elicits higher muscle activity than chair-sitting (ext 289). Ancestral movement was obligatory; modern movement is optional, bunched, and easily skipped. The mismatch is in HOW the day's muscle activity is spread, not in gross energy turnover.
parameters.resolution_unit: Incidental all-day movement woven into the fabric of living (errands, carrying, standing, walking between activities, active rest postures) - NOT a set-aside 'exercise' session. The functional target is the continuous distribution of low-level activity across waking hours, not weekly minutes of vigorous training.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Forager activity of over 100 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous movement and activity levels modestly above Western ones are found across populations (Pontzer, Wood and Raichlen 2018); the kilometre and rest figures are Hadza only.

evidence.author_quote: Among the many studies of the Hadza, one asked forty-six Hadza adults to wear lightweight heart rate monitors for several days. According to these sensors, the average adult Hadza spends a grand total of three hours and forty minutes a day doing light activities and two hours and fourteen minutes a day doing moderate or vigorous activities. Although these few hours of hustling and bustling per day make them about twelve times more active than the average American or European, by no stretch of the imagination could one characterize their workloads as backbreaking. On average, the women walk five miles a day and dig for several hours, whereas the men walk between seven and ten miles a day. And when they aren't being very active, they typically rest or do light work.

To put these values into context, hunter-gatherer PALs are about the same as those of factory workers and farmers in the developed world (1.8), and about 15 percent higher than PALs of people with desk jobs in developed countries (1.6). evidence.content: Physical Activity Level (PAL) data across populations reveals the surprising result that typical hunter-gatherers are only about 15% more active than industrialized people with desk jobs - equivalent to adding about an hour of exercise per day to a sedentary Westerner's routine.

Second, as recent technological and social developments have diminished industrialized people's need to be physically active, a growing chorus of experts has never ceased to raise the alarm that we aren't exercising enough.

evidence.author_quote: Many things surprised me when I first walked into a Hadza camp mid-morning on a torrid, sunny day in 2013, but I remember being especially struck by how everyone was apparently doing nothing. Hadza camps consist of a few temporary grass huts that blend in with the surrounding bushes. I didn't realize I had walked into a camp until I found myself amid about fifteen Hadza men, women, and children who were sitting on the ground as shown in figure 2. The women and children were relaxing on one side, and the men on another. One fellow was straightening some arrows, and a few children were toddling about, but no one was engaged in any hard work. To be sure, the Hadza weren't lounging on sofas, watching TV, munching potato chips, and sipping soda, but they were doing what so many health experts warn us to avoid: sitting.

evidence.author_quote: We have also medicalized exercise. By this I mean we pathologize a lack of physical activity, and we prescribe particular doses and types of exercise to help prevent and treat disease. The U.S. government recommends I engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate or 75 minutes of vigorous exercise a week and weight train at least twice a week. Epidemiologists have calculated that this level of activity will reduce my risk of dying prematurely by 50 percent and lower my chances of getting heart disease, Alzheimer's, and certain cancers by roughly 30 to 50 percent. Insurance companies offer me incentives to exercise, and entire professions have sprung up to motivate me to exercise in the first place, help me work out, and fix me up once I get injured.

parameters.name: Task diversity within the subsistence day
parameters.eea_baseline: The evolved exploratory-pursuit substrate (mesolimbic-dopamine SEEKING) is built for persistent inquisitive engagement with a varied environment, not for indefinitely repeating one narrow operation.
parameters.modern_default: Industrial and much digital work narrows the day to repetitive, specialized, often single-task operation - high repetition, low task variety, minimal novel problem-solving - with the SEEKING system left chronically under-stimulated by the work itself and frequently redirected onto engineered supernormal substitutes (feeds, games, variable-ratio rewards) off the clock.
parameters.gap_statement: The gap is the collapse from a high-variety, skill-diverse subsistence portfolio to narrow repetitive specialization, under-engaging the exploratory-pursuit system whose canonical evolved function is varied engagement with a changing world. No study in Cor measures forager task diversity.
parameters.resolution_unit: Genuine variety of self-directed, skill-recruiting tasks across the day that engage exploration and problem-solving - not nominal 'multitasking' (rapid switching among equally shallow operations) and not enrichment proxies bolted on outside the core work.

parameters.name: Daily subsistence work-hours
parameters.eea_baseline: No single daily work-hour figure is supported. The 'original affluent society' position (Sahlins, ext 714) reads the data as short food-quest hours and ample leisure. Data from the Alyawara showed that once food processing is counted, foragers spent far more time on getting food than those figures suggested (Hawkes and O'Connell 1981, ext 761). Ache men spent on average 6.5 hours a day acquiring and processing food in the forest (ext 2125). Agta adults spent on average 29.2% of daylight time on out-of-camp work, 24.0% on domestic chores, 12.2% on direct childcare and 34.7% at leisure, which counts socialising, resting, playing and sleeping (ext 2544). Lieberman writes that the Hadza workload is in no way backbreaking (ext 196), and typical hunter-gatherers are about 15% more active than industrialized people with desk jobs (ext 197). None of this licenses a specific daily work-hour figure.
parameters.modern_default: Modern work is organized around fixed, externally scheduled, boundary-less hours (clock-time labor, always-on digital availability).
parameters.gap_statement: The defensible mismatch is in the STRUCTURE of work-time (externally clocked, continuous, boundary-less vs. intermittent, self-paced, contingent), not in any claimed reduction or increase in daily hours.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (26 Nov 2026, the owner's answer to choice 7): tested once, per population. No single daily hour figure is supported. Once processing is counted, forager food-getting time is longer than the short-hours figures (Hawkes and O'Connell 1981, ext 761, the Alyawara). Among the Agta, camps doing more farm work had less leisure and more out-of-camp work (Dyble et al. 2019, ext 713). Main weakness: each figure is one population, and the Agta averages mix foraging and farming camps. The 'original affluent society' figures (Sahlins 1972, ext 714) are an argument.

evidence.author_quote: When Herman Pontzer and his colleagues measured daily energy expenditures in the Hadza, they were surprised to find that the highly active Hadza spend about the same total number of calories per day as sedentary industrialized people with the same lean body weight. In addition, when Pontzer and colleagues collected energetic data from adults in many countries including the United States, Ghana, Jamaica, and South Africa, they observed that more active people spent only slightly more calories per day than more sedentary people who weighed the same. In addition, individuals who were more physically active didn't have total energy budgets as high as their exertions would predict. How could someone who spent five hundred extra calories a day exercising not have a total energy budget that is five hundred calories higher? The proposed explanation is that people's total energy budgets are constrained: if I use five hundred extra calories walking, I'll spend less energy on my resting metabolism to help pay for my exertions.

parameters.name: Food diversity and seasonality (whole-food, micronutrient-dense, omnivorous variety)
parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral intake came from a wide, seasonally rotating array of wild plant and animal foods eaten in their whole, minimally altered form. Diet composition shifted with geography and season (ext 763); Eaton and Konner argue that it also shifted with period and kept the broad versatility typical of an omnivore (ext 38). Macronutrient and micronutrient profiles diverged sharply from the modern Western diet in nearly every measurable dimension at once: higher protein share, dramatically less refined carbohydrate and added sugar, lower sodium, higher potassium, higher micronutrient density, and near-zero industrially processed food.

eea_value.note: The 34% and 12% protein figures are model estimates (Eaton & Konner 1985, ext 39). Forager diets vary widely by habitat and season (Milton 2000, ext 763), and later reconstructions show wide ecological variation (Cordain et al. 2000, ext 729).

parameters.resolution_unit: Whole-food matrix and dietary variety, not any single 'good' or 'bad' nutrient: the mismatch is in the wholesale shift to refined, processed forms across the whole diet, not in one macronutrient ratio.

parameters.name: Satiety-honest fiber and whole-food matrix (food that signals fullness truthfully)
parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral foods were fibrous, so the volume and macronutrient signals reaching satiety circuits tracked the actual caloric load. Reconstructions place ancestral fiber intake far above modern levels (on the order of 100 g/day or somewhat more, Eaton 2006, ext 3605, vs ~20 g today, Eaton and Konner 1985, ext 39). Sweetness, fat, and salt arrived bundled inside a whole-food matrix, so the reward-system's responses to those cues were honest proxies for nutritional value. For the Hadza, honey is a favourite food and a substantial calorie share (Marlowe et al. 2014, ext 730).

eea_value.note: Fiber figures are reconstructions (Eaton 2006, ext 3605, which lowered the 100 to 150 g of Eaton & Konner 1985, ext 39).

parameters.modern_default: Ultra-processed, hyperpalatable products engineered to the 'bliss point', the mathematically optimized concentration of sugar, fat, and salt that maximizes craving. These foods decouple palatability from nutritional value and deliver calories faster, so the evolved fullness/reward proxies no longer track intake. Ultra-processed hyperpalatability is the modern proxy that defeats satiety.
parameters.gap_statement: Industrial formulation deliberately separates the reward cues (sweet/fat/salt) from the satiety cues (fiber, bulk, slow digestion) the two were ancestrally bundled together, so modern hyperpalatable food drives consumption past the point the body would otherwise stop, defeating the honest-signal logic of appetite regulation.
parameters.resolution_unit: Satiety-honesty of food (does palatability track nutritional/caloric load?), not calorie count alone: the failure is the engineered decoupling of reward from fullness, not merely high energy density.

parameters.name: Acquisition effort (calories are physically worked for)
parameters.eea_baseline: Food had to be physically acquired: walked to, foraged, dug, hunted, and processed. Among the Hadza, GPS-measured daily walking distances average about 11.4 km for men and 5.8 km for women (Pontzer et al. 2012, 30 adults over 11 days) and, in a larger sample of 179 people over 2,078 person-days, 12.9 km for men and 7.6 km for women (Wood et al. 2021, ext 3418), and women also spend several hours digging. This embeds substantial obligate movement and a real energetic and time cost between hunger and calories. Note: the absolute activity premium over sedentary moderns is modest (hunter-gatherer PAL ~1.8-1.9 vs ~1.6 for desk workers, ~15% higher), so the baseline is 'embedded all-day effort,' not extreme athleticism.

eea_value.note: Distances are GPS means for the Hadza (Pontzer et al. 2012). They are not work hours; for work hours see EEA-SUBS-04.

parameters.modern_default: Calories require essentially zero acquisition effort: hyperpalatable, energy-dense food is available on demand, pre-processed, with no movement, foraging, or processing cost between impulse and ingestion. The effort gate that historically bounded intake is gone.
parameters.gap_statement: Removing the work between hunger and food eliminates a natural brake on consumption and decouples eating from the obligate daily movement it was bundled with - calories are now frictionless to obtain and detached from the physical activity that ancestrally accompanied acquisition.
parameters.resolution_unit: Incidental, embedded, all-day acquisition movement (walking, foraging, carrying, digging) - NOT 'exercise' as a discrete bout. The mismatch is the loss of effort woven through daily food-getting, not a missing gym session. Work hours: see EEA-SUBS-04.

evidence.author_quote: Among the many studies of the Hadza, one asked forty-six Hadza adults to wear lightweight heart rate monitors for several days. Although these few hours of hustling and bustling per day make them about twelve times more active than the average American or European, by no stretch of the imagination could one characterize their workloads as backbreaking. On average, the women walk five miles a day and dig for several hours, whereas the men walk between seven and ten miles a day. And when they aren't being very active, they typically rest or do light work.

To put these values into context, hunter-gatherer PALs are about the same as those of factory workers and farmers in the developed world (1.8), and about 15 percent higher than PALs of people with desk jobs in developed countries (1.6). In other words, typical hunter-gatherers are about as physically active as Americans or Europeans who include about an hour of exercise in their daily routine. In case you are wondering, most mammals in the wild have PALs of 3.3 or more, nearly twice as high as hunter-gatherers. Thus, comparatively speaking, humans who must hunt and gather all the food they eat and make everything they own by hand are substantially less active than average free-ranging mammals.

parameters.name: Energy regulation is intake-bounded
parameters.eea_baseline: Total daily energy expenditure (TEE) increases with physical activity at low activity levels but plateaus at higher levels, after adjusting for body size and composition (ext 283). The authors' model has the body adapt to maintain TEE within a narrow range (ext 283). Pontzer and colleagues hypothesize that human daily energy expenditure may be an evolved physiological trait (ext 287), and write that population comparisons suggest it is an evolved, species-specific trait (ext 284). Hunter-gatherers and subsistence populations expend about the same total daily energy as industrialized adults of the same body size despite substantial differences in physical activity; the same wild-vs-captive constancy appears across mammals. Ancestrally, the binding constraint on energy balance was therefore food INTAKE (how much could be acquired and its composition), not how many calories activity could burn off.

eea_value.finding: TEE increases with physical activity at low activity levels but plateaus at higher levels, after adjusting for body size and composition (ext 283)
eea_value.implication: Obesity difference between Hadza and Westerners lies primarily in energy intake rather than expenditure.

parameters.modern_default: The lay model treats body weight as 'calories in minus calories out' with exercise as the lever for the 'out' side. Total expenditure rises with activity at low activity levels and plateaus at higher levels (ext 283): above moderate activity, each added ~100 counts per minute per day went with less than 50 kcal/day more expenditure. Above moderate activity this model fails: cranking up activity adds little to expenditure, while the intake side, driven by hyperpalatable, energy-dense, effortless food, is what has changed and what dysregulates energy balance.
parameters.gap_statement: Modern environments leave intake unbounded (cheap, hyperpalatable, effortless calories) while the body's expenditure stays homeostatically capped, so the one variable the system relied on as the binding constraint (limited, worked-for food) is exactly the one industrialization removed, and the popular 'just exercise it off' remedy targets the wrong, buffered side. Total energy expenditure increases with physical activity at low activity levels but plateaus at higher activity levels (ext 283).
parameters.resolution_unit: The binding constraint on energy balance: ancestrally INTAKE (food availability/composition), not expenditure. The mismatch is unbounded intake, not insufficient calorie-burning; exercise is a weak proxy for the metabolic problem.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade: tested many times. Total energy expenditure rises with activity at low levels and plateaus above moderate activity in doubly-labelled-water data from five populations (Pontzer et al. 2016, n=332, ext 283). Foragers and subsistence farmers expend about as much energy as people in industrial populations, and wild mammals about as much as captive ones (ext 284). The Hadza study found the same daily expenditure as in Western adults after controlling for body size (Pontzer et al. 2012, n=30, ext 286), which places the obesity difference primarily in energy intake rather than expenditure, and it proposes that daily energy expenditure is an evolved trait (ext 287). In trials, aerobic exercise alone took off 1.6 kg against controls at 6 months (14 trials, ext 3594), and 3.9 and 5.2 kg under 10 months of supervised sessions five days a week (Donnelly et al. 2013, ext 4028). The achieved energy deficit was in most trials smaller than the energy the prescribed exercise burned, and the authors conclude that the small weight loss comes mostly from low prescribed exercise doses together with eating more (Thomas et al. 2012, ext 4054); with intake held fixed, resting metabolic rate fell about 7 percent beyond what the weight lost accounts for (ext 4055).

We compared total energy expenditure, measured using doubly labeled water, against physical activity, measured using accelerometry, for a large (n = 332) sample of adults living in five populations. After adjusting for body size and composition, total energy expenditure was positively correlated with physical activity, but the relationship was markedly stronger over the lower range of physical activity. For subjects in the upper range of physical activity, total energy expenditure plateaued, supporting a Constrained total energy expenditure model.

parameters.name: Threat temporality (acute, episodic, escapable-by-action)
parameters.eea_baseline: Cacioppo and Patrick write that short, life-or-death confrontations drove the evolution of 'fight or flight' (ext 150). The fight-or-flight architecture was selected to spike hard and briefly, then terminate. Threat exposure was thus pulsatile, not continuous.
parameters.modern_default: Modern stressors are chronic and non-terminating: the overbearing boss, the long commute, financial precarity, abstract status anxiety, always-on connectivity. The same stressor persists hour after hour, year after year, while the sympathetic/parasympathetic architecture is unchanged. The threat system is engaged at a low chronic duty cycle it was never built to sustain, and the beneficial acute response becomes damaging on the chronic timescale.
parameters.gap_statement: The mismatch is in the time-course, not the threat machinery itself. The system is calibrated for brief, resolvable spikes; modern life supplies sustained, unresolved activation. Acute stress is adaptive (even enhances immunity); the identical response sustained chronically suppresses immunity and accumulates wear-and-tear. The gap is the absence of an episode boundary that lets the response shut down.
parameters.resolution_unit: Calibrate to threat TEMPORALITY (episode duration and duty cycle with a terminating standdown), not threat magnitude or count. A single intense-but-resolved spike is ancestral-normal; a mild-but-unending engagement is the mismatch. The unit is 'does the activation episode end and the system return to baseline,' not 'how scary was it.'
parameters.confidence_note: The acute-vs-chronic physiology is replicated in the corpus (Sapolsky id 331, graded replicated; McEwen id 130, graded cross_species): acute stress enhances and chronic stress suppresses immunity, and short-term vigilance changes that persist after the danger passes become maladaptive. The mismatch FRAMING (ancestral pulsatile vs modern continuous) is interpretive and rests on Cacioppo's prose (id 150, theoretical), so the row is graded argued, not yet tested, even though the underlying stress biology is well-replicated. No daily threat-frequency number is asserted. Uncontrollable threats were not rare in absolute terms. About half of forager children died before age 15 (Volk & Atkinson 2013, Evolution and Human Behavior 34(3):182-192, doi:10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2012.11.007: mean child mortality 48.8% across 20 hunter-gatherer samples, as coded by HRAF), and illness, which accounted for about 70% of deaths in pooled hunter-gatherer and forager-horticulturalist samples (ext 725), was a recurring threat that no individual action could resolve. Uncontrollable loss was still common.

evidence.author_quote: In contemporary society, as we've noted, most of our stressors do not come and go in the kind of short, life-or-death confrontations that drove the evolution of 'fight or flight.' We can have the same overbearing boss, the same long commute, the same worries about health care and retirement, and the same feelings of social isolation, hour after hour, year after year. Moreover, we now experience these persistent stressors over a life span that, on average, extends well beyond what was the norm during all but the last few centuries of our species' existence. The environment is entirely different now than it was in our environment of evolutionary adaptation

parameters.name: Threat controllability and predictability (resolvable by own action)
parameters.eea_baseline: The threat system evolved on the expectation that vigilance would be followed by an effective response that resolves the danger.
parameters.modern_default: Many modern stressors are structurally uncontrollable and unpredictable: algorithmic management and electronic monitoring strip decision latitude, outcomes hinge on systems no single action can move, and dread is open-ended (an unknown deadline, an unbounded threat). No behavior reliably terminates the stressor, producing the conditions for learned helplessness and chronic anticipatory dread.
parameters.gap_statement: The harm comes from uncontrollability and unpredictability, the absence of an action that resolves the danger, more than from threat itself. In a lab study of 32 adults waiting for shocks whose delay was shown in advance, nine preferred more voltage sooner to less voltage later (ext 4397), and Maier and Seligman write that learned helplessness in the laboratory, combining animal and human results, produced eight of the nine symptoms the DSM lists for depression (ext 442). Modern environments systematically supply unresolvable, action-proof stressors - the mismatch.
parameters.resolution_unit: Calibrate to CONTROLLABILITY = whether a behavioral response reliably terminates or averts the threat, not to mere familiarity or low intensity. A predictable-but-uncontrollable stressor (you see it coming, nothing you do helps) is the toxic case; an unfamiliar-but-action-resolvable one is ancestral-normal.
parameters.confidence_note: The controllability/predictability physiology is graded thin (Sapolsky id 333) and theoretical (learned-helplessness id 442). The EEA-baseline claim that ancestral threats were predominantly controllable is interpretive (no extraction quantifies ancestral controllability), so graded argued, not yet tested. Uncontrollable threats were not rare in absolute terms. About half of forager children died before age 15 (Volk & Atkinson 2013, Evolution and Human Behavior 34(3):182-192, doi:10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2012.11.007: mean child mortality 48.8% across 20 hunter-gatherer samples, as coded by HRAF), and illness, which accounted for about 70% of deaths in pooled hunter-gatherer and forager-horticulturalist samples (ext 725), was a recurring threat that no individual action could resolve. Uncontrollable loss was still common.

parameters.name: Real-vs-perceived threat ratio and all-clear resolution
parameters.eea_baseline: The smoke-detector logic produces many false alarms (a 1000:1 cost asymmetry makes ~999 false alarms per real escape optimal).
parameters.modern_default: The smoke-detector system keeps firing on cues it cannot resolve; social all-clear is attenuated by isolation. Activation that should be transient becomes chronic, shifting the body budget toward sustained inflammation and allostatic load.
parameters.gap_statement: Chronically unbalanced body budgeting and unbridled inflammation are implicated in chronic stress, in persistent anxious and low states (what Western scales score as anxiety and depression), and in physical disease (Barrett; McEwen allostatic load). The mismatch is the missing terminating action and missing social all-clear, not the false-alarm rate itself.
parameters.resolution_unit: Calibrate to RESOLVABILITY: a present threat that a behavioral all-clear (and a social all-clear via proximity/touch/reunion) can terminate - NOT bare threat count or alarm frequency. The ancestral system tolerated abundant false alarms; what it did not tolerate, and what modernity supplies, is alarms with no all-clear. The unit is 'can this activation be closed,' not 'how many alarms occur.'
parameters.confidence_note: Strong supporting physiology: the M8 allostatic-load chain is graded theoretical in McEwen id 469 and replicated in Sapolsky id 331, and the social all-clear is replicated (Coan/SBT handholding id 125). The integrative 'real-vs-perceived ratio with missing all-clear' framing is itself an interpretive mismatch synthesis, so graded theoretical, but it is the best-evidenced of the three threat rows on the downstream-immune side. The high false-alarm rate is presented as ancestral-normal (id 565, theoretical signal-detection formalization), not as a defect.

parameters.name: Killing between groups
parameters.eea_baseline: Lethal raids between groups occurred among foragers, and in some populations they were frequent. Killing between groups was part of the ancestral setting. Bowles compiled 23 sources and found war deaths averaged 14% of all deaths (archaeological 12%, ethnographic 16%; single sites 0% to 46%), in samples that include sedentary and contact-period groups, so his 14% is no forager default. Fry and Soderberg found that in 21 mobile forager band societies most of 148 recorded killings had one killer and one victim; about a third were between groups, but 38 of those 50 came from one society, the Tiwi, and in the other 20 societies about 15% were. A phylogenetic estimate puts all killing by other humans at about 2% of deaths.

eea_value.fry_soderberg_intergroup_share: about 15% of killings, excluding the Tiwi

parameters.modern_default: Killing between groups is done by states with armies.
parameters.gap_statement: The two headline numbers measure different things (share of all deaths in war, share of killings between groups) and cannot be averaged. A page can say lethal raids between groups occurred and were sometimes frequent; it cannot give one ancestral percentage.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (26 Nov 2026, the owner's answer to choice 7): tested many times that killing between groups was part of the ancestral setting: Bowles 2009 (ext 673, 1046), Fry and Soderberg 2013 (ext 674, 1047) and Wrangham and Glowacki 2012 (ext 672), independent groups. Main weakness: Bowles's samples include sedentary and contact-period groups, and burial samples may overstate violence, so his 14% is no forager default; Fry and Soderberg count the share of recorded killings, which gives no share of deaths. Gomez et al. 2016 (ext 675) is a phylogenetic estimate of all killing by other humans, about 2% of deaths. Choi and Bowles 2007 (ext 1058) is a model whose inputs come from Bowles 2009.

parameters.name: Signal provenance and accountability (information from known, reputation-bearing, face-to-face sources)
parameters.eea_baseline: Barkow lists mass communication and media and the ubiquity of strangers among the features of modern industrial societies that could not have existed in the Pleistocene (ext 2648). Boehm's ethnography of forager gossip describes a band that effectively keeps a running 'dossier' on every individual - provenance was the substrate of trust.
parameters.modern_default: The shift Tomasello describes - from face-to-face 'I-you' joint intentionality to impersonal 'we-as-group' collective intentionality - is taken to an extreme by mass and digital media, where signals are detached from any reputation-bearing source the receiver can sanction or even locate.
parameters.gap_statement: The evolved machinery for weighing information by source reputation and face-to-face accountability is deprived of the provenance cues it was calibrated to use. Receivers must evaluate high-stakes claims from sources they cannot place in any reputational web, and senders bear little reputational cost for deception - removing the gossip/ostracism feedback loop that ancestrally policed signal honesty.
parameters.resolution_unit: Proportion of consequential information arriving from a known, reputation-bearing, accountable source the receiver can locate and sanction - NOT raw access to information or number of contacts. A person can be flooded with information yet have almost none of it carry verifiable provenance.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): argued, not yet tested. No study measures where ancestral information came from; the claim that nearly all of it came from known people is inferred from band size and gossip ethnography. No published evidence argues the other way.

parameters.name: Gossip and narrative flow as reputation and norm transmission
parameters.eea_baseline: Among the Ju/'hoansi, daytime talk was mostly about economic matters, complaints and gossip, while firelight talk at night was mostly stories (ext 720). Gossip and narrative are talk about who behaved how, who is reliable or stingy, what happened, and what one ought to do. This stream did double duty - it transmitted norms, calibrated each person's reputation in the eyes of the group, and deterred free-riding because everyone knew gossip was constantly underway and anyone could become its subject. Boehm documents gossip, ridicule, and ostracism as enforcement against free-riders (bullies, the lazy, feigners, secret meat-eaters); Henrich notes that norm violations meant 'reputational damage, gossip, and a consequent loss of marriage opportunities and allies.'
parameters.modern_default: The tight loop in which gossip simultaneously informed, judged, and deterred within a single accountable group is broken: reputational narrative is broadcast without the reciprocal accountability that made it self-policing.
parameters.gap_statement: The gossip/narrative channel that ancestrally fused information transmission with reputation tracking and norm enforcement is decoupled. People consume reputational narrative about strangers they cannot sanction, and the norm-deterrence function (knowing the group is watching and will talk) is weakened in anonymous or one-to-many settings - leaving the evolved appetite for reputational narrative engaged but its enforcement payload disabled.
parameters.resolution_unit: Reputation/norm narrative circulating within a bounded group where subjects and audience are mutually known and can reciprocally sanction - NOT raw volume of social content consumed. Doomscrolling celebrity gossip is high-volume but supplies almost no actionable, reciprocal reputational signal.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Gossip, ridicule and ostracism as norm enforcement are documented across forager ethnography (Boehm 1993, 1999; Wiessner 2014) and gossip deters selfishness in experiments (Feinberg et al. 2012). That modern channels weaken this function is the framework's reading, untested.

Ethnographic accounts from forager, forager-horticulturalist and forager-pastoralist societies describe adults telling stories to teach children about the land, animals and proper behaviour, and describe stories that map places and warn of environmental hazards.

Across the ethnographic record of mobile foragers and many tribal groups, the group as a whole actively suppressed any member who tried to dominate, through ridicule, disobedience, desertion or, at the extreme, killing.
